name: Grace Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly it's labs and lectures for electrical engineering, about twenty hours, and then I'm in the library until it closes because my flat is loud. I live in student housing with five others, and on Saturdays I work at a bookshop called Pennywell, nine to five. It's tiring but I like it. I've never been this busy, and I keep forgetting to eat lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's been the hardest part of starting?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly the money. My mum is a nurse and my dad drives a city bus, and they pay part of my rent, but I can see Mum doing extra night shifts for it. I feel like I'm spending her sleep. So I'm careful with everything, and I got the degree I wanted, so I don't want to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, but quietly. My manager at Pennywell, Dee, keeps telling customers that AI will run everything, and I'd say it's mostly clever autocomplete. I wouldn't say it loudly though, because half my course already leans on it for coding labs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't fully trust the relief. My degree costs money my parents don't really have. Even if nothing changes, I still need a placement and then a graduate job, and those were hard to get before anyone mentioned AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Finish the circuits module, keep my Saturday shifts, and apply for a summer placement at the rail signalling firm that came to our open day. I still wouldn't touch the AI helper, even if it saved me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly, with a low hum of money worry. It's ordinary stuff like the loan, the rent and whether the placement comes through. AI isn't what keeps me up in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the AI helper even if it saved time. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In our first lab, a girl on my row got her whole code block from a chatbot and couldn't explain a line when the tutor asked. I would rather be slow and know it than fast and not be able to explain a single line. That's why I don't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your mum's overtime dried up, which bill would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my share of the food budget goes first, and then I'd ask Dee for extra shifts. I'd never tell Mum, because she'd try to cover it anyway. Dad's wage is steady but small, and my brother Owen, who's fourteen, always needs school trip money.

say: I'd tell friends that **AI is mostly hype**, and people are over-excited.
I'd say it quietly, because many on my course **use it already**.
think: I'm **relieved**, but my real worry is still **money** and finding a placement.
Nothing changing means the old problems stay: **loans**, rent and a tight job market.
do: Keep my **Saturday shifts** at the bookshop and finish the circuits module.
Apply to the rail signalling firm for a **summer placement**.
Carry on **not using** the AI helper in labs.
feel: **Steady**, with a low hum of money worry.
S0.quote: I would rather be slow and know it than fast and not be able to explain a single line.
fieldNote: Grace is firm about not using AI, and it comes from a **specific lab moment**, not a slogan.
Her worry is her mum's night shifts and the cost of her degree, more than technology.
She keeps her real view quiet in public, which shows a **small gap** between say and think.

steps.text: Keep working Saturday shifts at Pennywell bookshop
Apply for a summer placement at the rail signalling firm
Put part of each shift wage into a rent buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the students' union, because that's where I'd get heard. If AI takes over writing, checking and coding, then the companies saving money should pay something back. People shouldn't just be told to adapt while the owners keep the gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared for the entry-level jobs. Everyone tells me engineers are safe, but the entry-level jobs are the checking and drawing jobs, and those are the first ones a program takes. My degree is aimed straight at them, and I don't know where the starting rung goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd join the union branch properly instead of just paying the fee. I'd look hard for placements that involve site work, where someone has to be physically there. And I'd probably have to learn the tools after all, which I hate saying, because refusing completely might mean not getting hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. It feels like the rules changed after I'd paid my deposit. I do feel I have some control, because there's time and I'm good at the hands-on side of labs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools after all. How would you do that on your own terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I said I'd have to learn the tools, but I'd do it slowly and on my own terms. Maybe a short course through the union, not a chatbot at midnight. I want to be able to check what it's telling me, so I need the basics solid first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the change look from your mum's hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's hospital already uses software to schedule shifts, and the staff hate it. She says nobody asked them. If that's what the change is like, then I'd want a say before it lands on my degree too.

say: I'd say at the union that **firms saving money** should pay something back.
I'd say people shouldn't just be told to **adapt** while owners keep the gain.
think: The **entry-level jobs** my degree leads to are the checking and drawing jobs.
Refusing the tools completely might mean **not getting hired**, which I hate admitting.
do: Join the union branch **properly**, not just pay the fee.
Look for **site-based placements** where someone must be physically present.
Take a short **union-run course** on the tools.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit angry, as if the rules changed after I paid.
S1.quote: Everyone tells me engineers are safe, but the entry-level jobs are the checking and drawing jobs, and those are the first ones a program takes.
fieldNote: Grace blames **owners and firms**, not the technology, and wants collective answers.
She softens on learning the tools, but only slowly and with union backing.
Her mum's hospital scheduling software is her example of change **done to workers** without asking them.

steps.text: Go to union branch meetings every fortnight
Take a short union course on engineering software
Apply only to placements with site work
Do an extra evening module on site safety

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be at the students' union demanding emergency rules, honestly. Two years is nothing. Governments haven't even sorted social media, and now they'd need to rewrite how people earn a living. I'd say the companies building it must not decide alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. I finish my degree in 2029, and the jobs it leads to could be gone before then. My parents are borrowing against their little savings for part of it. By the time I get my degree, the jobs it was meant to lead to might not exist, and nobody will give back my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay on the course, because leaving feels like throwing it away. I'd ask the university what it plans to do, and I'd push for a public vote on rules. Practically I'd work more shifts at Pennywell, and I'd tell Mum and Dad not to spend any more on my fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel it in my chest every morning. I'm not frozen, but I don't have a plan, only a lot of small moves that might not add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents' jobs are hands-on. Does that change how you see their situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' jobs seem safer than mine, which is a strange thing to be grateful for. Nurses and drivers are physical, and robots come three years after the thinking part. But if the hospital cuts back on money because everything's changing, Mum's hours could still shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen, my brother, to stay calm and keep going at school. I'd say the world is changing but we'll sort it out together. I wouldn't say that I'm scared, because he's fourteen and watches everything I do.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules** and say the building companies shouldn't decide alone.
I'd say governments are **not ready** for how fast this would move.
think: I'm **frightened** that my degree jobs vanish before I graduate in 2029.
My parents have borrowed for my course, and the **loan** won't disappear if the jobs do.
do: Stay on the course but work **more shifts** at the bookshop.
Ask the university what it will do, and push for a **public vote**.
Tell my parents to **stop spending** on my fees.
feel: **Alarmed** every morning, with small moves but no real plan.
S2.quote: By the time I get my degree, the jobs it was meant to lead to might not exist, and nobody will give back my loan.
fieldNote: Grace links the threat directly to her **loan** and her parents' sacrifice, which makes it personal.
She has no plan beyond staying put and working more shifts, a sign of how little room she feels she has.
She protects her brother from her fear, which shows how she carries **family worry**.

steps.text: Add a second weekday shift at Pennywell bookshop
Ask the university for a meeting about its plans
Sign and share a petition for emergency AI rules
Stay on the engineering course for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning shot, and that five years is long enough to organise if people take it seriously. I'd say it at my union branch and to my mates in the flat. Some of them think I'm exaggerating, but they're doing the course where it hits hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm part of a squeezed group. Five years is long enough to finish my degree and short enough that I'd be the first generation to find the door shut. I'd have maybe two years in a job before the thinking work moves to machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but aim at the hands-on edge of engineering, like commissioning and site testing, where the robots arrive later. I'd save every placement wage. And I'd keep pushing in the union for a guarantee, like retraining paid by the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's like seeing weather coming on the hill. You can pull the washing in, but you can't stop the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned hands-on engineering work. How safe do you think that really is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I said hands-on edge, but I don't want to pretend that's safe forever. If robots catch up by 2034, even site work changes. What I'm really buying is time, a few years of earning, and a say in what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad drives a bus. Does this picture change anything for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives a bus, and he laughs about self-driving buses. I don't laugh. Five years might be enough for his depot to change, and then Mum's pay is the only steady one at home.

say: I'd call it a **warning shot** and say five years is enough to organise.
I'd tell flatmates not to laugh it off, even if they think I'm **exaggerating**.
think: I'd be in the **first generation** to find the door shut, with only two working years.
Even **site work** won't stay safe once robots catch up around 2034.
do: Finish the degree and aim at **commissioning and site testing** jobs.
**Save** every placement wage towards the loan.
Push the union for **paid retraining** guarantees.
feel: **Anxious**, like watching weather come in over the hill.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to finish my degree and short enough that I'd be the first generation to find the door shut.
fieldNote: Grace uses a **weather image** that shows how she feels: warned, but not able to stop it.
She is realistic that hands-on work is only a delay, not a shelter.
Her dad's bus depot makes the issue a **family-income** one, not only her own.

steps.text: Choose a final-year project in commissioning and testing
Save all placement wages for the student loan
Back the union demand for company-paid retraining
Talk with Mum and Dad about the household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't. It's enough time for law, for pensions, for retraining that actually works. I'd talk about it at the union and vote for anyone with a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel less terrified but more irritated. Ten years is enough time to fight for rules about who gets the benefit, if people bother to. I worry they won't, because it will feel far away until it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work a few years in practical engineering, and keep building savings. I'd probably learn the tools properly by my second year of working, because by then I'd understand the engineering underneath. And I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not the sharp fear of the fast one. It's more a long worry that everyone is waiting for someone else to deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools later. What stops that from becoming being left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've said I'd learn the tools later and slowly. With ten years that's actually reasonable, because I'm not forced to rush. My worry is that being slow turns into being left behind without noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother about what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen to learn things that need his hands and his head together, like a trade plus some theory. Not because I'm sure, but it keeps doors open. And I'd tell Mum she can retire a bit earlier if she wants, and we'd manage.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** if people use it for law and retraining.
I'd vote for anyone with a **real plan** and keep talking at the union.
think: I'd feel **less terrified** but irritated that people will wait until it's urgent.
My real fear is being **slow** and not noticing I've been left behind.
do: Finish the degree and work a few years in **practical engineering**.
Learn the tools properly in my **second working year**.
Stay in the **union** and keep building savings.
feel: **Uneasy**, a long worry that everyone is waiting for someone else.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to fight for rules about who gets the benefit, if people bother to.
fieldNote: The extra time **softens** Grace's stance on tools: she now says she would learn them, once she knows the engineering.
Her worry shifts from fear to **collective inaction**, which fits her progressive outlook.
She thinks of her brother Owen's future, so her plans reach beyond herself.

steps.text: Finish the electrical engineering degree on schedule
Learn engineering software tools in the second working year
Stay active in the union branch every term
Save a fixed amount every month for ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, no question. With two years there's no time for my degree, my parents' loan, or any rules to catch up. What would help is a government promise that students who started before the change won't carry the debt for jobs that vanished, and that unions get a seat when rules are written.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against technology. I'm against being told to trust it without being allowed to understand it. I'd rather learn the basics properly and know what I'm checking, and I'd like everyone else to be given the same chance.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against being told to trust it without being allowed to understand it.
portrait: Grace is an **18-year-old** electrical engineering student who works Saturdays at a bookshop and shares student housing.
Her parents, a nurse and a bus driver, pay part of her costs, and she **feels guilty** about her mum's extra shifts.
She is progressive and **resists** AI tools, and she blames owners and firms rather than the technology itself.
Her moods rise from uneasy to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks, and soften again with ten years.
She turns to **union and collective action**, and only slowly accepts learning the tools.
biggestWorry: The **fast** one worries her most, because her degree and her parents' money are tied together.
whatWouldHelp: A promise that students will **not carry debt** for jobs that vanish, and union seats when rules are written.
